title: Podcast Repurposing Readiness Score
subtitle: Find out how much you're leaving on the table from every episode you record.

questions.text: How often do you publish new podcast episodes?

answers.label: A few times a year at most
Once or twice a month, inconsistently
Monthly, fairly reliably
Weekly, most weeks
Weekly or more — it's built into my schedule

questions.text: How much of each episode's structure is decided before you hit record?

answers.label: I usually figure it out live
I have a rough idea but the episode shifts a lot
I follow a loose outline most of the time
I have a clear format I brief guests on
Every episode follows a defined structure built for repurposing

low.headline: Your podcast isn't a machine yet — and that's the real bottleneck.
low.text: You can't repurpose what you're not consistently recording. Everything else in this score depends on a steady stream of episodes. Nothing changes until the recording cadence is solid.
steps: Pick a cadence you can actually hold — once a month beats once a quarter you skip
Design a simple repeatable episode format before your next recording: same opening, same key segments, same close
Block one recurring calendar slot labeled 'record' and treat it like a client call

mid.headline: You're showing up, but the structure isn't designed for what comes after.
mid.text: Inconsistent structure is a repurposing tax. If every episode flows differently, every repurposing attempt starts from scratch. Fix the format, and repurposing gets faster every single time.
steps: Write down the repeating segments already in your episodes — make the invisible structure visible
Add one dedicated segment per episode designed to extract: a key takeaway, a one-liner, a story
Review your last three episodes and find where the structure broke down — fix that one thing first

high.headline: Solid foundation. The question now is whether your repurposing is keeping pace.
high.text: Your podcast runs reliably and the structure is clear. The only question left is whether you're extracting everything each episode is giving you.
steps: Map every segment of your standard episode format to a specific content format
Check whether your best old episodes have been fully mined — not just the recent ones
Add one dedicated episode moment designed specifically for a LinkedIn post hook

questions.text: After an episode publishes, how many different content formats do you create from it?

answers.label: Just the audio — maybe an episode link post
The audio plus one or two posts, inconsistently
2–4 formats: clips, a post, maybe a quote card
5–7 formats: clips, posts, carousel, newsletter section
7 or more formats extracted systematically from every episode

questions.text: How do you pull the best moments out of a recorded episode?

answers.label: I don't — I publish and move on
I pull something if a moment stands out while editing
I re-listen and manually note key moments
I follow a checklist or process after each episode
I have a repeatable system that runs every episode through the same extraction steps

questions.text: How much of your best content from past episodes is still sitting unused?

answers.label: Most of it — the archive is barely touched
A lot — I've shared a few things but no system for going back
Some — I pull from older episodes occasionally
Not much — I actively mine old episodes
Almost none — old episodes are part of my regular content rotation

questions.text: How many podcast episodes do you publish per month?
questions.hint: Count only episodes you actually published in the last 30 days

questions.text: How many pieces of content do you actually publish from a single episode (posts, clips, carousels, newsletters, quote cards)?
questions.hint: Count what you publish, not ideas you've had

low.headline: You're sitting on a content library you haven't opened.
low.text: Every episode you've recorded already has 7 to 10 LinkedIn posts inside it. The bottleneck isn't ideas — it's the extraction step. One episode, done right, should fuel your feed for a week.
steps: Pick one old episode and list every distinct insight, story, or quote in it
Turn one of those into a LinkedIn post today — just one, not a system
Set up a simple extraction template: key moment, one-liner, story, data point — what do you look for every time?

mid.headline: You're repurposing, but it's costing more effort than it should.
mid.text: The goal is a system where repurposing is the default, not the exception. If you have to decide what to do with an episode each time, the system isn't finished.
steps: Write out every step you currently take after an episode publishes — make the invisible process visible
Find the one format that takes longest and figure out how to cut that time in half
Set a number: how many pieces should every episode produce? Build toward that number consistently

high.headline: Your repurposing system is working. Now push the volume.
high.text: You're extracting well. The next lever is the archive. If you have 20 conversations and each has 5 posts in it, that's 100 pieces of content you haven't touched yet.
steps: Build a backlog from your 5 oldest episodes using your current extraction process
Track how many pieces each episode actually produces vs. how many it could
Add one new format to your repurposing checklist — the format you keep skipping

questions.text: How often does your podcast directly feed what you post on LinkedIn?

answers.label: Rarely — my LinkedIn and podcast operate mostly separately
Occasionally — when something obvious stands out from an episode
A few times a month from podcast content
Weekly — the podcast is a consistent source of LinkedIn posts
My podcast is my primary LinkedIn content source

questions.text: When you share a podcast moment on LinkedIn, how concrete and specific is the post?

answers.label: Generic — 'great conversation today, link in comments'
A brief description of the episode topic
One main idea from the episode, written into a post
A specific quote, moment, or story extracted and built into a post
Every piece is built around one precise insight the episode gave me

questions.text: When you sit down to post on LinkedIn, how often do you already know what you're writing about?

answers.label: Almost never — I wait until something comes to me
Sometimes — I try to think of something new each time
About half the time — I occasionally look back at episodes
Usually — my podcast gives me a running backlog of ideas
Always — I have more ideas from the podcast than I can use

low.headline: Your podcast and your LinkedIn are two separate things. They shouldn't be.
low.text: Your podcast is the hard part. Writing a LinkedIn post from something you already said out loud is the easy part. The connection between them isn't there yet — and that's the gap to close.
steps: Listen to your last episode and find one specific thing that was said that could become a post
Write that one thing this week — no episode link, no 'check out my podcast', just the idea
Do that for the next 4 episodes and track what your audience responds to

mid.headline: You're connecting podcast to LinkedIn. Now make the posts sharper.
mid.text: The link is working. The question now is specificity. Generic episode posts get scrolled past. Posts built on one precise moment, quote, or story from the conversation get read.
steps: For your next episode, find the single sharpest exchange or moment before you write anything
Write the post around that one moment — not the episode topic in general
Test: could this post exist without the episode? If yes, it's too generic — go more specific

high.headline: LinkedIn is running on podcast fuel. Keep the pipeline tight.
high.text: This is the model. Your podcast gives you the ideas; LinkedIn gets the output. The only risk is drifting toward generic — every post needs to be as concrete as the last.
steps: Review your last 10 LinkedIn posts: how many are built on a specific moment vs. a general topic?
If any are drifting generic, trace it back — what moment from that episode got skipped?
Consider posting more than one thing per episode — most conversations have 3 to 5 posts in them

questions.text: When you use AI in your content workflow, what role does it actually play?

answers.label: I don't use AI in my content process
I use it to write drafts and mostly publish what it gives me
I use it to speed things up but rewrite significantly
I use it to explore directions and options, then I decide what works
AI gives me more versions to compare — I always make the final call

questions.text: When AI helps you produce content, how much of the final piece sounds like you?

answers.label: Hard to say — it's a mix and I can't always tell
Close to me, but something's usually off
Most of it, after I edit enough
Consistently mine — I use tools but stay in control of the voice
Every piece is unmistakably mine — AI explores the options, I decide

questions.text: How do you decide which AI-generated version of something to keep?

answers.label: I pick whichever looks most polished
I go with what feels right in the moment
I compare options but don't have clear criteria
I know my voice well enough to filter AI output against it
I know what I'm testing, what worked, and why — AI is a direction machine, not a decision-maker

low.headline: If AI is making the call, it's working instead of you — not for you.
low.text: The point is more directions to explore, not a replacement for the judgment that makes your content yours. AI didn't make the creative decision for me in my best content work. It gave me more options to compare.
steps: Next time you use AI for a post, generate 3 versions instead of 1 — then pick and rewrite the best yourself
Write down 3 things that define your voice before generating anything — use those as your filter
If the final piece doesn't sound like something you'd say out loud, it goes back in

mid.headline: You're using AI as a tool, not a replacement. Keep the judgment with you.
mid.text: The difference between AI running your content and AI expanding your options is whether you're still in the decision seat. You're close — tighten the criteria you use to decide what stays.
steps: Before your next AI session, write down what you're actually testing: tone, structure, length, angle
Compare versions with that test in mind — not just feel
Edit what you keep until it passes a simple test: would you say this in a real conversation?

high.headline: AI is a direction machine for you — and that's exactly how it should work.
high.text: You're exploring more ideas without giving up the call. More directions to compare, you decide what works, and everything stays yours. That's how good content compounds over time.
steps: Document which AI-generated directions have worked best — patterns emerge over time
Apply the same exploration approach to older content: take an old post and run it through 3 new angles
Build a simple brief you hand to AI every session — same instructions, consistent output, you stay in control

questions.text: When you sit down to turn a podcast moment into a LinkedIn post, what does it feel like?

answers.label: Heavy — I overthink every word and often don't publish
Uncomfortable — there's pressure I haven't fully figured out
Manageable — I push through but it takes more energy than it should
Usually fine — I have a process that removes most of the friction
Easy — I have the idea from the episode, write one clear thing, and post it

questions.text: When a post underperforms, what actually happens?

answers.label: I take it personally and it slows me down for days
I feel deflated and it takes me a while to bounce back
I'm disappointed but move on within a day
I treat it as data and keep posting
Nothing changes — one post is one data point, not a verdict on the whole strategy

questions.text: How clearly do you know what you're going to say before you start writing a post?

answers.label: I usually start writing and hope it becomes clear
I have a rough direction but it shifts completely as I write
I have an idea but it takes a while to sharpen it
I start with one clear idea and write toward that
One episode moment equals one clear idea. I never start blank

low.headline: What's draining you isn't content. It's pressure.
low.text: Every post becomes a test. A judgement. A performance. That's what makes something simple feel heavy. The pressure comes from not having a process — so every post is treated like a statement. It's not burnout. It's friction.
steps: Your next post: one clear idea from your last episode, written in under 20 minutes, posted without a second reread
Post something that's just true, not perfect — see what happens
Time how long it actually takes to write a post — the number is almost always smaller than the dread

mid.headline: You're posting, but you're working harder than you need to.
mid.text: The friction isn't the writing. It's the decision about what to write. When your podcast gives you the idea, the post is already half-done. Use the episode as the brief — not the blank page.
steps: Before you write anything, write one sentence: what's the one thing from this episode that surprised me or cleared something up?
Write the post about that. One thing. Done.
Stop rereading before you post — you're editing in circles at that point

high.headline: You've got the mental game right. One idea, post it, move on.
high.text: That's the whole formula. And it's rarer than it should be. The system works because you stopped treating every post as a performance and started treating it as one clear thing you noticed and wrote down.
steps: Keep the cadence — the mental game compounds through consistency more than any individual post
If friction ever comes back, trace it: was the idea clear before you started writing?
Share the process openly — most people in your audience are still stuck in the overthinking loop
